nameStory: The name 'cormorant' comes from the Old French 'cormarenc,' meaning 'sea raven,' referring to their dark plumage and raven-like appearance. They're called 'great' because they're the largest cormorant species found in New England waters. In some places, they're simply called 'cormorant' since they're the most common species in the family.
description: Great Cormorants are large, dark waterbirds that look like a cross between a duck and a goose, but with a longer neck and hooked bill. These skilled diving birds are primarily black or dark brown with a distinctive yellow-orange throat pouch that's especially bright during breeding season. Adults typically measure about the size of a small goose, with a streamlined body built for underwater hunting. You'll often see them perched on rocks, docks, or buoys with their wings spread wide to dry their feathers.

idTips.label: Yellow throat pouch
idTips.description: A bright yellow-orange patch of bare skin at the base of the bill and extending down the throat, most vibrant during breeding season but visible year-round as a diagnostic field mark

idTips.label: Wing-spreading posture
idTips.description: Frequently seen standing upright with wings fully outstretched in a heraldic pose, looking like they're trying to dry laundry on a clothesline - a behavior unique among waterbirds

idTips.label: Hooked bill tip
idTips.description: Long, straight bill with a distinctly curved hook at the very tip, perfect for grasping slippery fish - you can see this hook even at a distance when the bird turns its head

idTips.label: Snake-like swimming
idTips.description: When swimming, only the head and curved neck show above water, creating an S-shaped silhouette that moves smoothly through the water like a swimming snake

idTips.label: Dark overall plumage
idTips.description: Appears almost black from a distance but shows subtle brown tones and slight iridescence up close, with feathers that often look wet and slicked-down even when dry

idTips.label: Heavy takeoff
idTips.description: Requires a long running start across the water surface to become airborne, flapping heavily and pattering their feet before finally lifting off - quite ungraceful compared to their underwater agility

habitat: Great Cormorants favor rocky coastlines, harbors, and estuaries throughout New England's maritime areas. You'll find them perching on jetties, channel markers, pier pilings, and rocky outcrops where they can easily access deep water for diving. They prefer areas with clear water and abundant fish, often near human infrastructure like docks and breakwaters.

seasonality.spring: Birds return to breeding areas with bright yellow throat pouches and may show white patches on flanks and thighs. Look for courtship displays and nest-building activities on coastal cliffs and islands.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season when adults are most colorful and active around nesting colonies. Young birds appear darker and duller than adults, lacking the bright throat coloration.
seasonality.fall: Large flocks may form as birds prepare for migration or winter movements. Adult breeding colors begin to fade, making the yellow throat pouch less prominent but still visible.
seasonality.winter: Many birds move south, but some remain in ice-free coastal waters. Winter plumage is duller overall, though the yellow throat pouch remains the key identifying feature year-round.

funFact: Great Cormorants are one of the few birds that can actually control their buoyancy underwater - they can partially deflate air sacs in their bodies to become less buoyant, allowing them to 'fly' underwater at depths of up to 150 feet while chasing fish, then reinflate to surface like a living submarine.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Double-crested Cormorants, but Great Cormorants are noticeably larger with a bright yellow (not orange) throat pouch and a thicker, more robust bill. Remember: 'Great' means both larger size and yellow throat - if it's smaller with an orange throat pouch, it's likely a Double-crested Cormorant.
contextualKnowledge: In some regions, Great Cormorants have faced persecution from fishermen who view them as competition for fish stocks, though studies show they primarily eat species not commonly sought by anglers. These birds have made a remarkable recovery in New England after being nearly eliminated by DDT and hunting pressure in the mid-20th century.
compareHints: As the only member of its specific genus regularly found in New England, Great Cormorants are best compared to Double-crested Cormorants, their closest local relatives. Great Cormorants are significantly larger and bulkier, with a thicker neck and more robust build overall. The yellow throat pouch versus orange, and the Great Cormorant's tendency to perch in more exposed coastal locations rather than inland waters, helps distinguish the two species.
